SGOIC looks to private-sector for information on America 250 Celebration spending in the territory

2026-11-24

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Senate Government Operations Investigative Committee last week continued its examination of the planning and financing of the Territory's America at 250 (A-250) celebrations, with lawmakers turning their attention to private-sector sponsorships and partnerships associated with the event.

During a hearing on Thursday, committee members questioned Nikolao Wendt, Chief Executive Officer of the Reid Group, about the company's role in supporting several activities held as part of the A-250 festivities.

The Reid Group includes several well-known local businesses, including Samoa Motors, GHC Reid, Peter E. Reid Stevedoring Inc., and Vaimalu Water.

Committee Chairman Senator Togiola Tulafono focused much of his questioning on how the partnership between the celebration's organizer, the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA), and the Reid Group was first established.

Wendt explained that his company had already been preparing activities for the Fourth of July before learning that the government and ASTCA were organizing a larger series of events to commemorate the A-250 celebration.

According to Wendt, company representatives approached ASTCA to discuss their plans, particularly a proposed Fourth of July car show, to ensure it would not conflict with any government-sponsored activities already being planned.

However, those discussions soon revealed that a much larger celebration was being organized.

"And that's when we were informed that there was a bigger plan for some bigger celebrations, and we were given the opportunity, or presented with the opportunity, to support more than what we had originally intended," Wendt told the committee.

He said the Reid Group subsequently agreed to partner with ASTCA on selected A-250 events, although the company was not involved in every activity connected to the celebration.

When asked whether ASTCA had provided specific conditions governing the company's participation, Wendt said several sponsorship opportunities were presented to them. He explained that the Reid Group chose to support events that aligned with the products and services offered by its various businesses.

Wendt also confirmed that he signed a formal agreement with ASTCA on behalf of the Reid Group outlining the company's participation in the festivities.

Chairman Senator Togiola Tulafono then asked whether the agreement required ASTCA and the Reid Group to split event expenses equally. Wendt confirmed that the company's share of the costs was calculated at $344,066.

According to Wendt, the Reid Group paid more than $50,000 directly to vendors involved in the events it co-sponsored. He explained that the remaining balance of the company's 50 percent share, totaling $288,915.20, was subsequently reimbursed to ASTCA.

Wendt testified that the reimbursement payment was made through Samoa Motors, a subsidiary of the Reid Group. He added that records documenting those payments were available and would be provided to the committee as part of its ongoing review of A-250 expenditures.

The testimony appeared to support earlier statements that ASTCA and the Reid Group had agreed to share the costs of the jointly sponsored events on a 50-50 basis.

The committee also requested additional documentation from the Reid Group. Togiola specifically asked Wendt to provide a list of vendors and service providers that were paid directly by the company in connection with the events it sponsored.

Wendt testified that before the celebrations, the Reid Group informed ASTCA of the products it intended to promote during the events.These included Vailima beer, Vaimalu bottled water, Active Pro, Powerade, and Coca-Cola products.

That disclosure drew the attention of Chairman Togiola, who noted that some A-250 activities were intended to promote anti-drug awareness and healthy lifestyles. He questioned whether the promotion of Vailima, an alcoholic beverage, was consistent with that message.

The committee also sought information about how private businesses became involved in the celebrations. Togiola asked Wendt whether he was aware of ASTCA soliciting businesses interested in using a government-sponsored event as a platform to market their companies or products.

Wendt responded that he was not aware of any such solicitation efforts by ASTCA.

During the hearing, however, committee members also acknowledged the Reid Group's long history of supporting community events across the Territory.

Senator Gaoteote Palaie Tofau thanked the company for its financial contributions to major public activities, including Flag Day celebrations. He encouraged the Reid Group to continue supporting community programs and, if possible, increase its assistance in the future, noting that such contributions help benefit the wider community.

ASCC awards Fall 2026 In-House Scholarships

2026-11-23

By

James Kneubuhl, ASCC Press Officer

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The American Samoa Community College (ASCC) makes available two “in house scholarships” open for application by all students at the College, one of which is also accessible to those who do not qualify for federal financial aid. The Division of Student Services, which administers the scholarships, has announced the recipients of the fall 2026 awards.

The Presidential Merit Scholarship, for which US citizens and nationals may apply, has been awarded to Mr. Lama J. Petelo and Ms. Oloitefumalevaipaepae Wilson. The Saili le Atamai SGA Non-Pell Scholarship, for which students born outside the United States and its territories may apply, has been awarded to Ms. Ruiyi Shi and Ms. Kuinilena Lofipo. For both these scholarships, the award takes the form of a $500 credit towards the recipient's tuition and fees at ASCC.

Applicants for the Presidential Merit Scholarship must be full-time students in the previous and current semesters and have maintained a grade point average of 3.60 or better. They need to have completed 24 credits towards an Associate Degree at ASCC, as well as the classes English 150, English 151 and Math 90. Applicants must be U.S citizens or nationals.

Presidential Merit recipient Lama J. Petelo, age 19, graduated from Manu’a High School last year and now majors in Liberal Arts at ASCC Mr. Petelo, a member of the PTK honor society, has previously served as president of the College’s Nursing Club. In the words of Languages & Literature instructor Ms. Jayleen Chun, “Lama is a well-rounded individual who balances academic rigor with a respectful, kind nature. Deeply rooted in his Samoan values, he is always the first to assist his peers or support his instructors.”

Ms. Oloitefumalevaipaepae “Olo” N. Wilson, age 20 and also a Presidential Merit scholarship recipient, graduated from Tafuna High School in 2024 and is pursuing a major in Pre-Law. As of fall 2026, Ms. Wilson has the honor of currently serving as president of two of ASCC’s three honor societies, the longstanding Phi Theta Kappa chapter as well as the Sigma Kappa Delta chapter, which focuses on English studies. “Olo represents the ideals of scholarship, leadership, service, and fellowship,” said Mr. Kuki Tuiasosopo, lead faculty advisor of the PTK honor society. “She has demonstrated that academic excellence and community leadership can go hand in hand. Her willingness to take on responsibility and represent her peers reflects a level of maturity that is commendable for a college student.”

The Saili le Atamai SGA Non-Pell Scholarship is sponsored by the ASCC Student Government Association and requires that applicants be full-time students in the previous and current semester with a grade point average of 3.0 or better, have completed 12 credits or more towards an Associate Degree or Certificate of Proficiency at ASCC, and have completed English 90 and Math 80. This scholarship is open for application by students who are born outside the United States and its territories who do not qualify for federal financial aid.

Saili le Atamai Scholarship Recipient Ms. Ruiyi Shi, age 28, was born in China and graduated from Fujian Changle No.3 Middle School in 2016. Although she has only been in American Samoa since 2024, Ms. Shi majors in Liberal Arts at ASCC, is on-track to graduate this semester, and has been accepted to attend the University of Hawaii at Manoa in spring 2027. “Instead of seeing my international background as a weakness,” she reflected, “I have learned to see it as an advantage because I can understand problems from more than one point of view. I now want to continue my education at a four-year university and build a career where I can use both my Chinese background and the experience I gained in the Pacific.”

Also awarded the Saili le Atamai Scholarship this semester, Ms. Kuinilena Lofipo, age 19, was born in the Independent State of Samoa, graduated from Samoana High School last year, and is now majoring in Elementary Education at ASCC. “As a non-Pell Grant recipient who receives no financial aid, Kuini understands the necessity of working twice as hard to fund her education,” observed Ms. Aioise Talamoni of the ASCC Admissions Office, where Ms. Lofipo serves in a work-study position. She also drew commendation from Teacher Education instructor Falanika C. Timoteo, who said of Ms. Lofipo, “Her academic commitment, positive character, responsibility, and willingness to support others demonstrate that she will continue to grow as a student and as a future educator.”

ASCC Dean of Student Services Dr. Emilia Le'i expressed her pride in the accomplishments of this semester's four In-House Scholarship recipients. The Dean also encouraged any ASCC students who were not selected for the scholarships to continue applying. “In 2026 we’ve seen an increase in the number of applicants for the In-House Scholarships,” she commented. “We take into consideration the situation of each student, their record of academic achievement, and their demonstration of good citizenship through community involvement.”

For more information on the ASCC In-House Scholarships, contact the Division of Student Services at 699-9155, ext. 0004.

Senator Muagututi'a, a dearly beloved father of the territory is mourned

2026-11-23

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — American Samoa has lost one of its most outspoken, respected and loved leaders with the passing of Senator Muagututi'a Moevasa Tauoa, a veteran lawmaker whose wisdom, courage, and unwavering commitment to public service earned him the admiration of colleagues and constituents alike.

Both the Senate president and Senate Pro Temp expressed their thoughts on the loss at the passing of the elder statesman.

SENATE PRESIDENT

Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean, who was informed by family members of the senator's passing Tuesday afternoon in Honolulu, described the loss as a heartbreaking one for the Territory.

"The Territory has lost a man of great wisdom and foresight," Tuaolo told local media.

Those who served alongside Muagututi'a often spoke of his honesty and fearlessness. He was known for speaking his mind, whether addressing fellow lawmakers, cabinet officials, or leaders in government. He believed that public office carried a sacred responsibility and never hesitated to remind others of their duty to serve the people faithfully.

"When Muagututi'a spoke, we listened," Tuaolo recalled. "He never sugar-coated his words. He said what was on his heart and what he believed needed to be said. Some people did not always appreciate being scolded by him, but that was the old man speaking as a caring father who wanted the best for his people."

SENATE PRO TEMP

Senate Pro Temp Magalei Logovi’i Magalei expressed that the loss of Senator Muagututi’a has created a profound void, particularly in the chambers of governance, where his empty seat now stands as a somber reminder of his absence.

Throughout his tenure, he was a source of wisdom and encouragement for those who served before the Senate, consistently emphasizing the importance of preserving and promoting our rich language, culture, and traditions. He championed the belief that these values should not only be remembered but also actively practiced and passed down to future generations.

He said that Senator Muagututi’a was a passionate advocate for preserving and promoting Samoan culture and language throughout his political career. He firmly believed the essence of Samoan identity should be maintained and often discouraged directors and officials from using English when testifying at hearings, stressing the importance of communicating in their native tongue to preserve cultural integrity.

HIS LEGACY

Senators and regular viewers of Senate hearings streamed on social media will remember several occasions when Senator Muagututi'a Moevasa Tauoa spoke with the blunt honesty that became his trademark.

Whenever an issue touched on the dignity of the Fono or the proper conduct of public officials, he rarely held back, choosing instead to say exactly what was on his mind.

One such moment occurred in March during a joint session of the Fono.

At the time, Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean informed lawmakers that Governor Pulaalii Nikolao Pula had requested a private meeting with him and House Speaker Savali Talavou Ale at Sadie's Restaurant. The Governor wanted to discuss the FY 2026 budget and the ongoing controversy surrounding funding for the salaries of unconfirmed cabinet directors.

Tuaolo told lawmakers he would only agree to the meeting if the Governor first removed his Chief of Staff, Leonard Seumanutafa. The demand followed a highly publicized confrontation inside the House of Representatives involving Seumanutafa and Vice Speaker Fetu Fetui Jr., an incident that had further strained relations between the Executive and Legislative branches.

While Speaker Savali initially expressed support for meeting with the Governor as requested, Senator Muagututi'a took a different view.

The veteran lawmaker agreed that discussions of such importance should not take place behind closed doors. In his opinion, any conversation involving the budget and other matters affecting the Territory should be conducted openly before the full Legislature, where all lawmakers could hear and participate.

He then turned his attention directly to the Speaker, delivering a rebuke that quickly became one of the most talked-about moments of that legislative session.

"Please, Speaker Savali, do not politicize this situation by meeting with the Governor privately," Muagututi'a said. "You have been doing that kind of thing ever since you entered the Fono many years ago, and you are still doing it. The Fono is the institution where matters affecting the wellbeing of the Territory are to be addressed. Stop it."

The chamber immediately erupted in laughter, easing some of the tension created by the senator's unusually direct remarks. Yet beneath the laughter was a serious message. Muagututi'a's comments reflected his longstanding belief that government business should be conducted openly and that the Legislature should never be sidelined when major decisions affecting the people of American Samoa were being discussed.

If there was one final moment that captured Senator Muagututi'a's uncompromising style, it came in September during a Senate session when he delivered what would become his last major public rebuke from the Senate floor.

The veteran senator launched into a fiery address in Samoan that evolved into an extraordinary condemnation of Governor Pulaali'i Nikolao Pula, culminating in a direct appeal to voters to remove the governor from office. For many longtime observers of the Fono, it was vintage Muagututi'a: blunt, fearless, and unapologetic.

His outburst was triggered by the governor's decision to dissolve the Board of Directors of the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA), a move that had already generated controversy and raised questions among lawmakers.

Addressing his fellow senators, Muagututi'a accused the governor of repeatedly disregarding the authority of the Legislature and acting beyond the limits of his office.

"I have monitored the Governor's actions from the beginning," Muagututi'a declared in a stern tone. "We should not be afraid to tell him that he has overstepped his authority because we put him where he is. How many times has he gone against the Fono's decisions? We should not be afraid of him."

In a dramatic moment, the senator turned toward the camera broadcasting the proceedings live to viewers on the Senate website and social media platforms and addressed the governor directly.

"Pula, if you are watching this broadcast, I'm telling you now that you are full of disrespect," he said. "I remind you that the government consists of three branches, the Executive, Legislature, and Judiciary. I am certain a significant amount of funds have been misused, and that is the reason he has dissolved the Board."

The speech then took an even more personal turn as Muagututi'a questioned the governor's conduct and leadership style, arguing that public office required humility, accountability, and respect for both the law and Samoan customs.

"Pula, you have been disrespectful and rude to the people of this Territory," the senator said. "This is what happens when someone who has been living off-island becomes a matai and is not fully versed in the responsibilities that come with that title, especially respect."

Muagututi'a also expressed disappointment over what he viewed as the governor's treatment of Lt. Governor Pulu Ae Ae Jr., questioning the dynamics within the administration and suggesting that elected leaders should place the interests of the people above personal or political considerations.

"Why did you select Pulu as your Lt. Governor and now you disrespect him?" he asked. "This is not your government that you can rule from wherever in the world you travel to. This is the government of Tutuila and Manu'a. We should elect a governor who truly cares for the people of American Samoa. Change the governor. Don't vote for Pula."

The remarks were broadcast live and quickly circulated across social media, generating strong reactions from supporters and critics alike.

Some viewed the speech as an inappropriate personal attack, while others saw it as an example of Muagututi'a's willingness to say publicly what many were reluctant to express themselves. Samoa News understands many of his fellow senators also disapproved of his remarks, characterizing them as showboating by the Sua County senator.

However, regardless of where people stood politically, few doubted the sincerity behind his words.

Throughout his years of public service, Muagututi'a saw himself as a guardian of the Fono's constitutional role and an outspoken defender of government accountability. He believed senators had a duty to challenge authority when they believed the public interest was at stake, even if doing so invited criticism.

In many ways, the September speech embodied the qualities for which he will be remembered: a fierce independence, an unwavering confidence, a deep attachment to Samoan values, and a willingness to confront powerful figures head-on.

It serves as a final reminder of a senator who rarely measured his words and who, until the end, remained determined to speak his mind.

Within the Senate, Muagututi'a was regarded by many as one of the chamber's elder statesmen. His presence commanded respect, and younger lawmakers often looked to him for guidance. According to Tuaolo, his absence had already been deeply felt during recent Fono sessions while he was away receiving medical treatment.

A passionate defender of Samoan culture and language, Muagututi'a was a firm believer that the Samoan language should remain at the center of government proceedings. During committee hearings, he frequently encouraged government directors and officials to testify in Samoan, emphasizing the importance of preserving the language and ensuring that the work of government remained rooted in Samoan identity.

He was equally passionate about leadership and accountability. During confirmation hearings for cabinet nominees, Muagututi'a often reminded appointees that they were among the "birds of the flock" who had been sent away to gain education and experience and had now returned home to serve their people. His advice was straightforward and consistent: be honest, serve the public first, treat every employee fairly, and never show favoritism.

While his voice has now been silenced, the values he championed, respect for culture, honest leadership, accountability in government, and service to the people, will remain part of his enduring legacy.

A native of Faga'itua, Muagututi'a served the people of Sua County in the Senate for nearly a decade after first being elected in 2016 and subsequently re-elected to continue his service. He was serving in his third term when he passed.

The management and staff of Samoa News extend their deepest condolences to his family, the people of Sua County, and all those whose lives were touched by his leadership. May he rest in peace.

ASCC-SGA hosts Fall 2026 Career Fair

2026-11-20

By

James Kneubuhl, ASCC Press Officer

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA  — The Student Government Association (SGA) at the American Samoa Community College (ASCC) hosted its fall 2026 Career Fair on Tuesday, November 9th. With this event, the SGA assists students seeking local and federal opportunities to begin a career or looking for internships and summer jobs.

Now a regular event every spring and fall semester at ASCC, the Career Fair typically features representatives from more than a dozen businesses and other organizations in the public and private sector meeting one-on-one with students to inform them of available opportunities along with any requirements involved. This semester, the SGA recorded 146 students taking part in the two-hour event, which took place in the College’s Multi-Purpose Center auditorium.

SGA Coordinator Ms. Falaileato Suiaunoa explained that more than a month of preparation goes into the Career Fair.

“As a group, the SGA deliberates on which departments, businesses and organizations we invite. Our SGA President is involved in creating an invitation letter and gathering information. Invitation letters usually go out four to six weeks in advance, after which we follow-up regularly. On the day of the event, we maintain constant contact with all the vendors that come. Hosting the Career Fair provides a valuable opportunity for the SGA to develop their leadership, communication and collaboration skills.”

Asked about the effectiveness of the Career Fair, Ms. Suiaunoa described feedback received from participating businesses and agencies as “very positive and helpful.”

As she explained, “We have had students set up job interviews and even secure positions as a result of the Career Fair. We just recently began the survey process with our vendors and agencies, but the earliest results indicate the Career Fair definitely helps employers and students connect. Also, since we began utilizing our ASG Human Resources and programs like WIOA, these entities have been very helpful in assisting our students with summer jobs.”

Participants in this semester’s ASCC Career Fair included the American Samoa Visitors Bureau; Department of Human and Social Services; Public Works; the National Parks; American Samoa Legal Aid; American Samoa Telecommunications Authority; the US Army- 9th Mission Support Command; Utah National Guard; Back on Track; PIOA Consulting and Engineering; ASCC Teacher Education Department and Lumana’i Educators Association; American Samoa Human Resources/ Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act; Bluesky; US Marine Corps; Department of Homeland Security; American Samoa Democratic Party; ASCC Human Resources; National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association; and the Christopher James Foeoletini Ledoux Foundation.

For more information on the American Samoa Community College and its many opportunities and services, visit the College’s website at: www.amsamoa.edu.

Owner of Continental Transport Corporation expresses frustration with location setbacks

2026-11-20

Says its not only with Zoning Board, but also with Industrial Park management

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — For more than three decades, Continental Transport Corporation (CTC) has been a familiar name in American Samoa's construction industry, supplying building materials and providing services that support both government and private-sector projects. Today, however, the company finds itself at a crossroads.

After being denied permission twice by the American Samoa Zoning Board to relocate its retail and production operations, CTC owner Tony Togia'i says he is running out of options.

Frustrated by the repeated setbacks, Togia'i is now faced with the challenge of finding a suitable location where his company can resume full operations, continue serving customers, and generate enough revenue to pay employees, meet financial obligations, and keep the business afloat.

The CTC owner complained that their predicament is especially frustrating given his company's long service to the territory's development and infrastructure needs since the mid-1990s.

For more than a decade, CTC operated from its production and retail headquarters in Fogagogo near Maliu Mai Beach Resort, where it supplied construction materials and provided a range of services to contractors, homeowners, and government agencies. That chapter came to an end in 2025 when the company's lease expired and was not renewed.

Following the loss of its Fogagogo facility, Togia'i sought alternative locations that could accommodate CTC's extensive operations. Among the options pursued was space at the government-owned Senator Daniel K. Inouye Industrial Park in Tafuna.

Togia'i recalled that he had previously approached local businessman and Tool Shop owner Peter Crispin about the possibility of subleasing the last lot on the street near the turnoff adjacent to NAPA Auto Parts and across from the Department of Public Works (DPW) compound. The property had previously been occupied by an ice manufacturing company, and Crispin had acquired the lease from the former operators. According to Togia'i, Crispin was receptive to the proposal and indicated that he would consider the request and get back to him. However, he never received a response.

Seeking other options, Togia'i turned to Uili Leauanae, Deputy Director of the Department of Commerce (DOC). He said Leauanae informed him that there were no available lots within the Industrial Park that could accommodate the company's needs, leaving CTC with limited alternatives for relocating its operations.

Leauanae subsequently advised him that three vacant one-acre government lots were available for lease in the Vailoa-Leone area commonly known as the "Airstrip," and suggested that the company pursue the necessary approvals to secure one of the sites. According to Togia'i, Leauanae advised him to apply for a zoning variance and pursue a government lease for the property.

The area derives its nickname from the former Leone Airfield, a World War II-era military airstrip constructed by the U.S. Navy. The airfield once encompassed what are now several well-known landmarks, including Leone High School, Midkiff Elementary School, and the site of the former WVUV 648- AM radio station. Although the airfield was abandoned in early 1945 because of turbulent wind conditions and limited operational use, the area continues to be popularly known as the "Airstrip."

However, the proposal encountered strong opposition from nearby residents, who argued that the operation would pose significant environmental risks and potentially endanger public health and safety, particularly for students attending the two neighboring public schools. Their concerns ultimately played a major role in the Zoning Board's decision to deny CTC's application for a zoning variance.

The company's most recent setback came earlier this month when the Zoning Board again rejected a variance application, this time for a proposed site in Tula on communal land belonging to CTC owner Tony Togia'i's family.

The denial followed objections raised by a resident whose home is located downwind of the proposed facility. Togia'i noted that he had submitted a petition supporting the project that was signed by several residents living near the proposed site, but the board ultimately sided with the concerns raised by the opposing resident.

A frustrated Togia'i told Samoa News that he felt his predicament was unfair. He said he fully understood why the Zoning Board denied his application for a zoning variance at the Airstrip site in Vailoa, given its close proximity to homes, schools, and government facilities. He noted that several residents had submitted written objections, while others appeared in person at the board's public hearing to voice their concerns.

However, Togia'i argued that the board's decision to reject his most recent application for a brick-manufacturing facility on his family's communal land in Tula was far more difficult to understand. He pointed out that the denial was based largely on the objection of a single resident whose home was not located in the immediate vicinity of the proposed site.

According to Togia'i, the board gave greater weight to that opposition than to a petition supporting the project that had been signed by several residents whose homes are adjacent to the proposed location. He said those residents would be the most directly affected by the operation and had no objection to the project moving forward. He stated that he was going to submit a request for reconsideration to the Zoning Board.

The disgruntled CTC owner said he has already invested heavily in the venture and must now begin searching for yet another suitable location. He estimated that he has spent approximately $50,000 on state-of-the-art equipment for the manufacture of concrete bricks and tri-bars, large reinforced concrete structures commonly used as wave breakers and shoreline protection barriers to help control coastal erosion and safeguard infrastructure from storm-driven waves.

"I've tried every available option that was suggested to me, but each one has led to another dead end," Togia'i said. "Now I have to start all over again looking for a place where I can operate."

Togia'i said he was particularly disappointed by the board's decision because CTC is one of only two local companies manufacturing concrete bricks in the Territory, the other being CBT/ Builders Hub.

According to Togia'i, major hardware retailers such as Ace Hardware and Tool Shop currently import much of their brick supply from Fiji. He said CTC's bricks were sent to Fiji for independent quality testing and exceeded the required standards.

The favorable test results, he added, led Ace Hardware to enter into a special arrangement with CTC under which the company would serve as Ace's exclusive local supplier of concrete bricks.

Togia'i argued that supporting local manufacturing would help reduce reliance on imported construction materials while creating economic opportunities within the Territory. He noted that CTC had already invested heavily in equipment and production capabilities in anticipation of growing demand for locally made bricks and other concrete products.

The CTC owner also expressed frustration with what he described as the government's management of the Senator Daniel K. Inouye Industrial Park. Togia'i argued that greater priority should be given to local manufacturing and construction companies such as CTC, which he said has spent more than five decades serving the people of American Samoa and contributing to the Territory's economy.

Instead, he claimed that industrial park lots are often awarded to high-ranking government officials, their relatives, and businesses from outside the Territory, while established local companies struggle to secure suitable sites for expansion.

"Surely more than 50 years of service and contributing to the Territory's economy should mean something," a disappointed Togia'i said. "It is very discouraging to see lots at the Daniel K. Inouye Industrial Park sitting idle, with lessees doing nothing with them or simply subleasing them to other businesses.

"It has also come to my attention that some lessees owe thousands of dollars in unpaid lease payments and are still allowed to operate. The sad part is that some of them are top government officials and prominent members of the community.

"Meanwhile, CTC, a company that my grandfather built from the ground up and which has grown into a household name in the construction and manufacturing industry, is not being given a fair opportunity to expand and grow."

LOCAL FAMILY-COMMUNITY ROOTS

Continental Transport Corporation (CTC) is one of American Samoa's larger locally owned construction and aggregate-supply companies. The company's roots go back to 1968, when the late Nu'utele Tiamo Togia'i started a small retail store and operated a single four-wheel bus.

After returning to American Samoa in 1970, his son, Fa'asefulu Togia'i, and wife, Elisapeta Togia'i, expanded the business, developing agricultural operations and growing the transportation side of the company. Over time, the business grew into a fleet of about 35 buses, becoming a major transportation provider on the eastern side of Tutuila. It was during this period that the company became known as Continental Transport Corporation (CTC).

In the mid-1990s, the family sold the bus transportation operation and shifted the company's focus to heavy construction. Starting with a dump truck, excavator, and backhoe, CTC expanded into earthmoving, infrastructure construction, aggregate production, equipment rentals, concrete production, and related services.

At present, CTC's operations extend well beyond general construction work. The company specializes in the production, retail sale, hauling, and storage of cinders, sand, rock aggregates, and other construction materials that are essential to infrastructure and development projects throughout the territory. It also provides laboratory testing services for construction materials, rents heavy equipment, performs truck and machinery maintenance and repairs, and manufactures concrete products used in both public and private construction projects.

Togia'i said the most suitable location for CTC's proposed brick and tri-bar manufacturing operation would be the stretch of industrial lots across from Veterans Memorial Stadium along Airport Road. The area is already home to similar heavy industrial activities, including a quarry operated by local contractor Paramount Builders. Just one lot away, McConnell Dowell, a construction and engineering company founded in New Zealand, operates a stone-crushing quarry and related facilities. The company has maintained a longstanding presence in American Samoa and has been involved in numerous public infrastructure projects throughout the Territory.

According to Togia'i, the lot situated between Paramount Builders and McConnell Dowell has remained vacant and undeveloped for years. He said he inquired about the possibility of leasing the property, only to discover that the lease is registered under the surname of a high-ranking government official.

"I don't know if the official himself is the lessee or if it's a relative," Togia'i said. "What I do know is that the lot has been sitting there unused for years while companies that actually need the land to create jobs and produce local products can't get access to it."

The lots along this section of Airport Road fall under the jurisdiction of the Department of Port Administration (DPA). They are also located within the broader area targeted for future development under the airport modernization component of the Vision 2030 initiative being advanced by DPA Director Barney Sene. Vision 2030 envisions a series of long-term improvements to airport infrastructure and surrounding properties, including commercial development opportunities, terminal upgrades, cargo-handling facilities, and other projects intended to support economic growth and modernize transportation infrastructure.

Togia'i acknowledged the importance of long-term development planning but questioned why strategically located industrial lots continue to sit idle while local companies seeking to expand their operations struggle to secure suitable sites.

"If the goal is economic development, then local businesses that have invested in American Samoa for generations should be part of that vision," he said. "We're ready to build, ready to hire, and ready to produce locally. All we're asking for is a fair opportunity."

via RNZ National News

Newly established Opioid and Substance Abuse Council holds first meeting

2026-11-19

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The inaugural meeting of the newly established Opioid and Substance Abuse Council (OSAC) was convened last Friday by Governor Pulaaliʻi Nikolao Pula and Lieutenant Governor Pulumataala Ae Ae Jr. at the Governor's Office in Malaeoletalu, Fagatogo.

The meeting brought together government officials, healthcare professionals, law enforcement representatives, religious leaders, and community stakeholders to confront what many consider one of American Samoa's most pressing public health and public safety challenges.

The event also marked the beginning of a long-overdue coordinated effort to develop long-term strategies aimed at reducing substance abuse, strengthening treatment and recovery services, and preventing illegal drugs from reaching the Territory.

Representatives from the Office of the Attorney General, the Department of Health, Department of Public Safety (DPS), Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and several community organizations participated in discussions focused on the effective use of opioid settlement funds and the creation of a comprehensive territory-wide response to substance abuse.

Officials described the council as a vehicle for bringing together agencies and community partners that have often worked independently on related issues. The goal is to improve coordination, share information, and ensure resources are directed toward programs that produce measurable results.

A significant portion of the discussion centered on efforts to curb the introduction of illegal drugs into American Samoa, particularly through ports of entry and the U.S. Postal Service. Council members stressed that reducing the local availability of illicit substances must remain a cornerstone of the Territory's anti-drug strategy.

The issue takes on added importance following changes in territorial law enacted by the Fono last year. Under the new law, responsibility for investigating and enforcing drug smuggling cases intercepted at seaports, the airport, and through the postal system has largely shifted from the Department of Public Safety (DPS) to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Previously, DPS served as the lead agency in nearly all drug interdiction cases. The legislative change was intended to strengthen border security efforts by placing greater responsibility on DHS, whose mission includes protecting the Territory's borders and points of entry.

However, questions remain regarding the Territory's readiness to address emerging threats, particularly the possibility of fentanyl reaching American Samoa.

During a Senate hearing last month, Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean questioned Homeland Security Director Vaetagaloa Glenn Lefiti about the department's preparedness to prevent fentanyl and other dangerous narcotics from entering the Territory.

In response, Vaetagaloa acknowledged that DHS currently lacks some of the resources necessary to effectively combat the threat, noting that additional funding, equipment, and personnel would be needed to fully carry out the department's expanded enforcement responsibilities.

The concerns raised during that hearing highlighted the importance of close cooperation among law enforcement agencies, health officials, and policymakers as the Territory seeks to strengthen its defenses against increasingly sophisticated drug trafficking operations. The concerns were also raised with Governor Pulaali'i during his October 14, 2026 press conference. In response, the Governor explained that shortly after his administration took office in 2025, DHS Director Vaetagaloa approached him seeking American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding to support the department's operations.

Governor Pulaali'i said he learned that during the tenure of former DHS director, the late Samana Semo Ve'ave'a, the department had received little to no financial assistance. He noted that this situation came to light four years after American Samoa received ARPA funding from the federal government in 2021.

“As a result, I allocated $8 million from our office's ARPA funds to DHS,” Governor Pulaali'i said. “The department used the money to construct an access road to Mount Alava, allowing personnel to more easily reach the antennas and other communications equipment located there. The project was intended to help ensure uninterrupted communications with the U.S. DHS and other relevant agencies throughout the mainland United States and the Pacific region.”

However, the Governor noted that the project sparked disagreement with the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA). According to Pulaali'i, ASTCA's director maintained that matters involving telecommunications infrastructure fall under the authority's jurisdiction, raising questions about whether the project should have been overseen by the local DHS or ASTCA.

During Friday's meeting, council members emphasized that enforcement alone cannot solve the problem. Participants agreed that prevention, education, treatment, and rehabilitation must play equally important roles in any long-term solution.

One initiative highlighted during the meeting was the Department of Health's ARPA-funded Drug Rehabilitation Facility, which is currently under construction. Once completed, the facility is expected to provide much-needed local treatment services for individuals struggling with addiction, reducing the need for families to send loved ones off-island for care and recovery.

(Samoa News should point out that the drug rehabilitation facility project is facing possible funding problems if the use of ARPA funds is not extended from its current December 31, 2026 deadline. The project is seeking an extension to May 2027.)

Members also discussed the importance of improving data-sharing among government agencies to better identify trends, track drug-related incidents, and coordinate responses. Enhanced communication between health professionals, educators, law enforcement officers, and community organizations was identified as essential for early intervention and effective prevention efforts.

To support these goals, the council established specialized working groups that will focus on public education, prevention programs, treatment services, and community outreach. Particular emphasis will be placed on reaching young people through schools, churches, youth organizations, and village-based programs designed to raise awareness of the dangers associated with drug use and addiction.

Governor Pulaali'i and Lt. Gov. Pulu emphasized that lasting success will require the active participation of the entire community. They encouraged churches, village leaders, nonprofit organizations, and families to become partners in the effort to protect future generations from the devastating consequences of substance abuse.

The newly appointed members of the Opioid and Substance Abuse Council include Assistant Attorney General Louise H. Lafitaga; Deputy Commissioner of DPS Lauti Tautalasoʻo Moliga; Department of Health psychiatrist Dr. Peni Biukoto; DHS Director Vaetagaloa; Deputy Treasurer Levi Reese; clinical psychologist Dr. Jueta (Eta) B. McCutchan; Reverend Iasepi Ulu; and community representative Ipu Lefiti.

The council is expected to meet regularly as it develops policies and recommendations aimed at creating a safer, healthier, and drug-free American Samoa.

Deep-sea mining auctions spark environmental concerns in American Samoa and Northern Mariana Islands

2026-11-19

By

The Associated Press

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka sat in the shallows at Fatumafuti Beach as her 4-year-old daughter, Erhys, splashed through the clear water on a Little Mermaid kickboard. Below, iridescent blue and rainbow-streaked fish wove through fields of coral.

It was a rare moment of calm before a long journey. Soon, Suluai-Mahuka would travel from American Samoa to California to protest the Trump administration’s efforts to lease areas near her island for deep-sea mining. She planned to pack a bottle of seawater that would give members of the Samoan diaspora a chance to touch and connect with the waters she’s fighting to protect.

The administration has taken a major step forward this year in promoting deep-sea mining by scheduling a series of auctions of the U.S. seafloor. The first waters it is targeting are some of the most pristine areas of the Pacific Ocean near American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands, two U.S. territories thousands of miles from where decisions for their islands are being made.

Despite its status as an experimental and controversial industry, deep-sea mining has become a pillar of President Donald Trump’s campaign to expand U.S. control over minerals critical to the technology and defense industries. In April last year, the president directed his administration to expedite the search for those metals on the ocean floor, both within and beyond U.S. borders. Auctions for the seabed near Virginia and Alaska could take place next year, while the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is reviewing permit applications from companies that seek to mine in international waters.

The minerals companies are after include nickel, cobalt, manganese and copper — useful to making everything from smartphones to electric vehicles — that have concentrated over millions of years along the ocean floor and the volcanic crusts of seamounts. It’s unclear how abundant they are near American Samoa and the Northern Marianas.

In granting a lease, the U.S. would be joining a handful of other countries that have allowed companies to start exploring their waters for deep-sea minerals. Most mining techniques involve deploying underwater vehicles thousands of feet deep to vacuum up rocks and sediment from the ocean floor. Under most proposals, those rocks are filtered and returned to a mining ship, with unwanted debris released back into the ocean.

Suluai-Mahuka and other opponents have tried to stall the auctions of the nearby ocean, rallying public comments criticizing the move. They are prepared to work against the obstacles that come with living in territories dependent on federal aid, where residents have neither a voting representative in Congress nor the right to vote for president.

“When they ask us for public comments, it always feels like we’re just screaming at a moving train,” said David Cabrera, who leads a group seeking to revive Indigenous forms of fishing in Saipan, the main island of the Northern Marianas.

Located in the Pacific Ocean between Hawaii and Australia, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands are two separate chains of volcanic islands that both endured occupations by colonial powers before becoming U.S. territories.

Despite economic challenges and a diaspora that is slowly shrinking their populations of 50,000 people, the territories have kept alive traditions that tie them to the ocean and remain sacred to the Indigenous peoples who first made the region’s islands home.

The U.S. waters surrounding American Samoa include Rose Atoll, an uninhabited island named for the pinkish hue of its coral reefs that is an important habitat for seabirds. The U.S. waters around the Northern Marianas include parts of the Mariana Trench, the deepest place on earth. Both are protected by marine monuments that now border the proposed mining areas.

If a lease is granted, it will be difficult to undo under a different administration, said former Bureau of Ocean Energy Management Director Elizabeth Klein. The government would have to justify the cancellation at a hearing and face potential litigation.

In response to the mounting opposition, the newly formed Marine Minerals Administration has emphasized that the upcoming auctions will only grant companies the right to take initial steps to explore for seafloor minerals. Any testing or commercial mining proposals will go through further public comment and a more intensive environmental review.

“It’s cold comfort,” said Zeno Camacho Deleon Guerrero Jr., a resident of the Northern Mariana Islands and a board member of the Micronesia Climate Change Alliance, a nonprofit focused on protecting the region’s environment and people. “Once you find what you want, you’re going to get it. You’re going to start mining.”

American Samoans fear irreparable losses to their way of life

The first auction for deep-sea mining — in waters near American Samoa — was scheduled to take place Thursday in the Southern California city of Thousand Oaks.

Suluai-Mahuka had decided to be in California, despite the long hours it would take to get there. She and her team at Finafinau, the environmental group she founded, were working to bring people from across the Pacific community to protest alongside them.

“If these people are going to be selling our ocean, they’re going to see our faces when they do these bids,” she said.

A legal battle now makes it unclear whether the auction will proceed. On Monday, a judge ruled the government violated the Endangered Species Act by failing to consider the full impacts of a deep-sea mining lease. By Wednesday morning, the Trump administration had yet to delay the auction. Two other lawsuits are pending.

For an opening bid of $3 million, the administration was offering companies the chance to vie for 20-year leases granting them the exclusive right to mine commercially if approved in further environmental reviews. Two areas of the seafloor, each more than 15 million acres in size, were available for bidding.

The administration has proposed another auction for five parcels of the seafloor near the Northern Mariana Islands in December.

Deep-sea mining goes against everything Suluai-Mahuka stands for, she said, and against the Samoan way of life that revolves around the ocean — whether it’s diving among corals, swimming and relaxing, fishing for local delicacies, or the commercial tuna industry that sustains the local economy. All of that, to her, is at risk.

“We would be giving up a piece of ourselves that we cannot get back,” she said. Her group, Finafinau, takes its name from the Samoan word for resilience.

In Samoan legend, the world began as only the heavens and the ocean.

“The ocean is life. It’s sacred to us,” said Malouamaua Tuiolosega. “We lose the ocean, we lose life.”

Tuiolosega represents the ancient governing council of Manu’a, a district of American Samoa that makes up the closest inhabited areas to where deep-sea mining leases could be granted, about 100 nautical miles from its shores. Populated by just 800 people across three islands, and isolated by infrequent transportation to the capital city of Pago Pago, Manu’a residents depend even more heavily on the environment for survival.

Since long before American Samoa became part of the United States, the council’s chiefs have overseen the islands’ resources, which they understand are in delicate balance with people.

If more is taken from the islands than is needed to survive, Tuiolosega said, “you violate the relationship and the trust between the people and its resource, and then it disappears.”

He sees the same push toward exploiting the oceans behind deep-sea mining as he does the Trump administration’s efforts to open up marine monuments in the Pacific Ocean to commercial fishing. The governing council, the Faleula o le Manu’atele, has joined one of the lawsuits against the Trump administration over the upcoming lease sale.

“President Trump recognizes the enormous potential of America’s offshore critical minerals to drive technological innovation, economic prosperity, and national security,” Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement to The Associated Press.

“A lease sale is not a mandate to mine. Any future extraction would require additional environmental review and regulatory approvals, informed by engagement with local communities,” Rogers said.

Although no company worldwide has started commercial mining operations in the deep sea, a crop of U.S. startups, buoyed by the president’s policies, hopes to soon change that. Some supporters believe deep-sea mining could be an important income stream for American Samoa if it were to become an industry hub.

“If we don’t look for some kind of manufacturing process, something that people will buy, we’re going to be destitute. We’re going to be broke,” said John Wasko, executive director of the American Samoa Economic Development Council, a group promoting industry on the islands.

The deep-sea mining startup Impossible Metals, which has signaled interest in the upcoming auction, has offered to share 1% of any future profits with the American Samoan community.

Suluai-Mahuka and others don’t buy the promises of jobs and investments.

The leases offered by the Marine Minerals Administration will ask companies to “make every reasonable effort” to hire employees from the territories and support “community well-being,” but the regulations don’t include any binding requirements or numeric targets.

There is also no guarantee of economic gains. While the federal government would collect the winning bid amount, along with regular rent payments and royalties over the life of the lease, there are no mandates for the government to share earnings from deep-sea mining with local territories or states. That’s different from offshore oil and gas drilling, where Gulf states receive 37.5% of revenue.

Questions go unanswered for local government

A major question for local government is whether a deep-sea mining lease will hurt American Samoa’s tuna fishery and force the closure of the last remaining cannery. Purse seine and longline fleets supply tuna for the local StarKist plant, with the longline fleet fishing entirely in U.S. waters — including the areas up for leasing.

Nathan Ilaoa, director of the American Samoa Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources, said his agency was hoping for a “more exhaustive” review of the potential impacts to the fishery before the auction. He said he doesn’t yet have answers on whether contaminants or sediment plumes from disrupting the ocean floor will alter the tuna’s migratory patterns.

“We’re extremely concerned that the disappearance of our longline fleet could translate into the cannery leaving American Samoa, which would be an economic disaster for the territory,” Ilaoa said.

American Samoa’s leadership opposed deep-sea mining when word of company interest started reaching its shores. In 2024, the territory issued a moratorium on deep-sea mining in the waters it controls, which extend from shore out to 3 nautical miles (5.5 kms). But the territory has little say over the activities that take place in federal waters beyond that line.

When the auction was proposed last year, American Samoa Gov. Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, a Republican, wrote to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management that he and all chambers of local government unanimously opposed deep-sea mining, as did the vast majority of residents. But the governor now welcomes the auction, according to a Monday statement.

“This is a historic moment for American Samoa and for our nation,” he said.

A spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration said it has carefully considered feedback from the governor of American Samoa, and will incorporate it into the agency's process “to the maximum extent practicable,” including sharing the locations of deep-sea mining ships, coordinating with fishing vessels, and reviewing any impacts to fish habitat.

The agency said it supports sharing deep-sea mining revenues with territories, and is working with lawmakers and Department of the Interior leadership to support changes that would grant it the authority to do so.

It did not respond to questions about why the auction was arranged to be thousands of miles from American Samoa, or how it factored in local opposition to its policies on deep-sea mining.

In the Northern Mariana Islands, it’s an overwhelming time to fight back

Residents of the Northern Mariana Islands are closely watching the events in American Samoa as they brace for a potential auction of the seabed near their islands. The proposal has come at a challenging time for the territory, which was battered by two super typhoons in April and July.

The territory’s government is in fiscal crisis, with Gov. David M. Apatang warning of austerity measures after a five-day shutdown in October. Many public schools suffered broken windows and damaged roofs from the storms, while residents face rising electricity costs from the territory’s sole energy provider.

“It’s very overwhelming for everybody here in this region right now,” said Cabrera, the advocate for traditional fishing. “You just want to worry about keeping your lights on and putting food on the table, so it’s a challenge to get support for anything other than that.”

Born and raised in Saipan, and descended from the Indigenous Carolinian and Chamorro peoples, Cabrera served in the U.S. Navy for seven years and worked in the United States mainland before returning home. He founded his group, Talaya Club, to teach people on the island how to fish with traditional fishing nets known as talayas that are cast out in the ocean surf.

His long-term goal is to help island families become less dependent on imported food through traditional fishing. Sediment plumes from deep-sea mining near the Northern Mariana Islands could endanger that mission, he said.

“That will inevitably impact our fisheries and the health of our fisheries, and thus the health of our people,” Cabrera said.

Residents of Saipan have already waged many fights against the U.S. government. Most recently, islanders objected to U.S. Navy plans to turn the territory’s beloved island of Pagan into a firing range for thousands of troops. The agency formally abandoned those plans in July after more than a decade of community pushback.

When the deep-sea mining auction was proposed, the Northern Marianas government initially reacted with a measured tone. Both Apatang, an independent, and Kimberlyn King-Hinds, the Republican nonvoting congressional delegate, said they neither supported nor opposed deep-sea mining.

But after the federal government doubled the leasing area in March to include waters both east and west of the territory, Apatang opposed the auction, according to Henry Hofschneider, the governor’s chief of staff. The expanded leasing area is just 57 miles from Saipan and 46 miles from the U.S. territory of Guam.

Still, the governor said in a statement to the AP that he has faith in the rule of law and believes federal regulations will protect the marine environment from harm. He has asked the Marine Minerals Administration to consider pausing the auction until the various lawsuits have been heard and decided. In September, King-Hinds introduced a bill in the U.S. House that seeks to distribute 50% of federal deep-sea mining revenues to the nearest territories.

Cecilio Raiukiulipiy worries that deep-sea mining threatens another tradition in the Northern Marianas — navigation by the sea and stars.

Raiukiulipiy was granted the title of navigator in a special ceremony in 2018. Once you accept the title, he said, “it’s your responsibility to keep the knowledge, to pass it on, and to take care of your people, all the people in the islands and also the environment.”

Several times per year, his voyages take him across the Mariana Trench, adjacent to where the Trump administration could green-light seabed mining. On the western side of the trench, he said, the water is colder and the waves churn like a washing machine. It’s an area home to “all kinds of whales,” and where seafood come to spawn, he said. He has seen baby eels swimming north toward the waters of Japan.

“Those are indicators that we are on the right course,” he said. Known as seamarks, or living waypoints, they are derived from a deep-seated knowledge of the seaways in his part of the world.

Raiukiulipiy belongs to one of the groups suing the Trump administration to try to stop the auction off the Northern Marianas next month.

“They don’t understand how we live,” Raiukiulipiy said of the federal government in Washington. “They’re looking at it with a dollar sign. Us, we look at how we’re going to survive, how we are going to live, how we are going to eat.”

Like many around him, the ocean is also sacred to Raiukiulipiy. His community believes their ancestors come from deep in the ocean.

“We usually do our burials in the ocean,” he said. “We bury them back.”

Port Administration graduates five new law enforcement officers

2026-11-18

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Port Administration of American Samoa (PAAS) proudly welcomed five newly sworn officers into its ranks during the PAAS Law Enforcement Academy graduation ceremony held on Friday, November 13, 2026.

The five graduating cadets—Officer Lefiti, Officer Lualua, Officer Matala, Officer Moananu, and Officer Snow—successfully completed rigorous training to bolster safety, security, and public service across American Samoa’s air and sea ports.

Acting Commissioner of Public Safety Lauti Tautalaso'o Moliga served as the ceremony's keynote speaker, sharing words of encouragement and emphasizing the core values of integrity, vigilance, and dedication to the community. Following his address, Acting Commissioner Moliga officially administered the Oath of Office, inducting the five graduates into active duty.

PAAS Director Barney Sene delivered the closing remarks, commending the graduates for their perseverance and highlighting the critical role they will play in safeguarding the territory's primary gateways. “You have finally reached this monumental milestone in your career that took months to achieve.”, said Director Sene. “It was not easy. Your new role as Law Enforcement Officers grants you certain powers and many responsibilities to carry out your duties. The powers granted onto you to enforce laws can be misused and abused. I caution all of you to be careful. Be humble and know that you are here to serve and protect the people, not the other way around. Honesty and integrity are pillars you need to uphold everyday at work and in your lives. Remember who you serve. The people.”

The PAAS Law Enforcement Academy (PLEA) process started in January 2026 with 174 applicants. The number was whittled down to 94 qualified applicants. The 94 applicants were then given a multiple choice and written test on general math and English comprehension skills. 27 individuals passed the test with a grade of 80% or above. The 27 individuals were then given a Physical Test (PT) of which 13 passed and moved into the full 4-month PLEA.

At the successful completion of the 4-month classroom instruction, hands on training, and required certifications, 8 individuals remained to enter the On the Job Training (OJT) portion of the Academy. Coming into the PLEA graduation today, only 5 individuals have reached the end point. A 5% success rate from the original 94 applicants. “We want quality applicants at Port. We go through a rigorous process to ensure the Law Enforcement Officers (LEO) we train and bring into Port are mentally, physically and emotionally qualified to perform the job,” said Director Sene.

The PAAS Law Enforcement Academy equips recruits with specialized skills in port security, emergency response, regulatory compliance, and community policing to ensure safe and efficient operations for residents, travelers, and commerce.

House Agriculture Committee visits Samoa on fact-finding trip of poultry industry

2026-11-18

Sees the success of the strong partnership between private sector and govt

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — A group of American Samoa lawmakers returned recently after a weeklong visit to Samoa with a clear message: while the poultry industry in the neighboring island nation is rapidly expanding and investing in large-scale production, the territory remains heavily dependent on imported eggs and poultry products to meet local demand.

That was the consensus shared by members of the House Agriculture Committee following their seven-day fact-finding trip to Samoa. The delegation was led by Committee Chairman Tiaoalii Fauagiga Sai and included Vice Chairman Ape Mike Asifoa and committee member Representative Luaitaua Gene Pan. They were accompanied by Samoa Consul General in American Samoa, Fata Brian Kaio, and House Counsel Seiuli Alvin Tuala.

According to the lawmakers, the visit provided a firsthand look at the significant growth taking place in Samoa's agricultural sector, particularly in poultry production. The delegation toured farming operations, met with industry representatives, and discussed opportunities for greater collaboration between the two Samoas.

They noted that Samoa has made substantial investments in modern poultry facilities and is steadily increasing its capacity to supply locally produced eggs and chicken products, reducing its dependence on imports while creating new economic opportunities for local farmers and businesses.

The lawmakers said the trip highlighted the contrast between Samoa's expanding poultry industry and American Samoa's continued reliance on imported poultry products, raising important questions about food security, agricultural development, and the potential for strengthening local production in the territory.

Led by major agri-business operators such as the Frankie and Ah Liki groups, Samoa's poultry industry has experienced significant growth in recent years. With strong backing from the Samoa Government and its agricultural development programs, producers have invested heavily in modern poultry facilities, expanded egg production, and increased local chicken meat processing in an effort to reduce the country's reliance on imported poultry products.

Lawmakers who visited Samoa said the industry's rapid expansion reflects a coordinated strategy between the government and private sector to strengthen food security, create jobs, and keep more food production within the country. They noted that large-scale poultry farms are now producing substantial quantities of eggs and chicken products, helping Samoa move closer to meeting local demand through domestic production rather than imports.

Sunshine Pacific Farm, a subsidiary of Frankie's Company Ltd., is one of Samoa's largest commercial poultry operations. The company built poultry houses in Tanumalala for egg production in 2019 with a capacity of about 19,500 birds, added more poultry houses in 2021, and now has the capacity to produce up to 3,000 dozen eggs per day.

The success of Samoa's growing poultry industry was also highlighted by Taimalie Charlie Westerlund, owner of Tanumapua Poultry Farm, which is part of the Ah Liki Investment Group. Speaking with members of the delegation, Westerlund proudly pointed to the farm's achievements, noting that its locally produced eggs now account for approximately 75 percent of egg sales in Samoa's retail market.

Westerlund said consumer demand for locally produced eggs continues to grow because of their freshness and quality, giving them a competitive edge over imported products.

"Our eggs are of higher quality, healthier, and certainly much fresher than imported eggs," Westerlund said. "Consumers can tell the difference. At the same time, we're offering them at very reasonable prices, which makes locally produced eggs an attractive option for families and businesses alike."

The American Samoa delegation, who tasted the eggs every morning during their one-week visit, agreed wholeheartedly.

"They were delicious," said an impressed Representative Ape Mike Asifoa said. "The Samoa poultry industry is a success story that American Samoa would do well to emulate."

According to Asifoa, the delegation was informed that Samoa's rapidly growing poultry sector has reached a stage where locally produced eggs now supply the vast majority of the domestic market, dramatically reducing the country's dependence on imported eggs. He said industry leaders are confident that, with continued investment and government support, Samoa is on track to achieve full self-sufficiency in egg production in the near future.

"The level of growth we witnessed was remarkable," Asifoa said. "What stood out most was the strong partnership between the government and private sector. Their efforts are producing real results, and the country is now far less reliant on imported eggs than it was just a few years ago. They are very close to being able to meet all local demand with eggs produced right there in Samoa."

In contrast, he pointed out that there is very little large-scale commercial poultry production in American Samoa. Most chicken meat and eggs are imported, although there are some small local producers and backyard operations. The sole official egg production operation, the Taputimu Farm Fresh Eggs located in Taputimu village, is owned by Bill and Nancy Satele and has been operating since 1976.

Despite the presence of a long-established local egg farm, American Samoa has been unable to produce enough eggs to satisfy territory-wide demand. Industry observers point to high feed costs, shipping expenses, limited economies of scale, labor shortages, and other operational challenges as major obstacles to expanding local production, leaving the territory heavily dependent on imported eggs.

The local chicken meat farm and processing plant at Mulifanua is also growing rapidly, and lawmakers were told that if the sector continues its current trajectory, it could create new economic opportunities for villages, church groups, community organizations, and individual families interested in poultry farming.

Industry representatives explained that the two major companies driving the sector have developed a partnership model designed to benefit both the businesses and local communities. Under the arrangement, interested groups and individuals can purchase young chickens from the companies and raise them on their own farms using feeding programs and animal-care practices recommended by company technicians.

This is important as the chickens used in the operation are specially bred meat-producing birds, commonly known as broilers, which are imported from overseas. These birds are specifically developed for rapid growth, efficient feed conversion, and high meat yield, allowing them to reach market weight in a relatively short period of time. Unlike traditional village chickens raised primarily for eggs or household consumption, broilers are bred exclusively for commercial meat production.

Broilers are imported when they are one day old and are fed and nurtured until they are strong enough to be sold to interested community members. Once they reach market size, the farmers can then sell them back to the company for processing, packaging, and distribution. The system provides a guaranteed market for growers while enabling the companies to increase production without having to raise all of the birds themselves.

According to those involved in the industry, the approach has the potential to generate new sources of income for families and village communities while helping Samoa expand local chicken meat production and reduce its reliance on imported poultry products. Members of Parliament were told that the model is also benefiting constituencies by creating economic activity at the grassroots level and allowing more people to participate directly in the country's growing poultry industry.

Representative Asifoa described the delegation's visit to Sunshine Pacific's chicken meat farm and processing plant at Mulifanua as an eye-opening experience that underscored the importance of a strong partnership between government and the private sector.

He said the operation demonstrated how coordinated investments in agriculture cannot only stimulate economic growth but also strengthen a country's food security and resilience in the face of unforeseen disruptions.

According to Asifoa, discussions with Samoa's Minister for Agriculture and Fisheries, Fuimaono Maiava Tito Asafo, and Ministry Chief Executive Officer Afamasaga Taimalietane Matatumua focused on fostering closer cooperation between the two Samoas and exploring pathways to facilitate the export of fresh Samoan eggs and poultry products to American Samoa.

However, Asifoa noted that the primary challenge remains compliance with the requirements of the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS), which regulates the importation of animal products into the United States and its territories to prevent the introduction and spread of poultry diseases.

He said ministry officials informed the delegation that Samoa has not yet submitted a formal application seeking approval to export its poultry products to American Samoa. Despite this, Asifoa stressed that the visit highlighted valuable lessons for the territory and reinforced the need for American Samoa's Department of Agriculture to take a more proactive role in developing the local poultry industry.

"We cannot continue relying almost entirely on imported food products," Asifoa said. "What we saw in Samoa shows what can be achieved when government and private businesses work together toward a common goal. Developing our own poultry industry will not only improve food security but could also create new economic opportunities for families, community groups, and entrepreneurs throughout the territory."

He emphasized that expanding local egg and poultry production should be viewed as a long-term investment in American Samoa's food security and self-sufficiency.

Asifoa noted that recent global and transportation-related events highlight the vulnerability of island communities that rely heavily on imported goods.

He pointed to the recent Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) order grounding departing flights across the United States due to safety concerns, as well as the ongoing conflict involving Iran, as examples of situations that can disrupt international transportation networks. Such events, he said, can have a ripple effect on American Samoa by affecting shipping schedules, delaying cargo deliveries, and potentially reducing the availability of essential imported goods on local store shelves.

"The government needs to be prepared," he emphasized. "It doesn't hurt to be prepared, but it will certainly hurt if we are not prepared." He said the territory cannot afford to wait until a supply-chain crisis occurs before taking steps to strengthen local food production and reduce its dependence on imported goods.

via RNZ National News

Am Samoa Bar Association holds first High School Mock Trial Competition

2026-11-16

Students try a fictional murder case as ASBA sets its sights on the 2028 Nationals

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The American Samoa Bar Association (ASBA) congratulates the students, coaches and schools who took part in the inaugural American Samoa High School Mock Trial Competition, which concluded on November 12 with a championship round at the High Court of American Samoa.

Tafuna High School and Samoana High School met in the final, with Samoana High School named the champion.

Eight teams from seven schools competed: Faga'itua High School (FHS), Leone High School (LHS), Manumalo Baptist High School (MBHS), Nu'uuli Vocational Technical High School (NVTHS), two teams from Pacific Horizon High School (PHHS), Samoana High School (SHS) and Tafuna High School (THS).

Students stepped into the roles of attorneys, witnesses, clerks and bailiffs to try a fictional criminal case — American Samoa Government v. Olena Molia. In the case, restaurant owner Olena Molia is charged with first-degree murder in the death of her business partner, Toni Lua, at their restaurant in Tafuna.

The prosecution argues that Molia acted after discovering that Lua had been stealing from the business, and that she stood to gain half a million dollars from her partner's death. The defense contends that someone else is responsible, pointing to a loan shark to whom Lua owed more than two hundred thousand dollars.

The case featured six witnesses and twelve exhibits, and teams had to be ready to argue either side.

The preliminary rounds were held on November 2 at the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Courthouse, where NVTHS, MBHS, SHS, and THS advanced.

In the semifinals on November 3, also at the ALJ Courthouse, THS defeated MBHS and SHS defeated NVTHS. The championship round followed on Nov. 12th at the High Court.

Students were scored on their preparation, communication and courtroom performance rather than on the legal merits of the case.

Attorney General Gwen Tauiliili-Langkilde and La'apui Ale judged the first day of competition. Administrative Law Judge Roy Hall presided over the semifinals, and Associate Justice Sunia and Acting Associate Justice Patea judged the championship final.

“Mock trial gives our students something a classroom cannot: the experience of standing in a real courtroom, thinking on their feet, and making their case with respect for the other side,” said ASBA President Lornalei Meredith. “The young people we saw this month showed the confidence and character our community needs, whether or not they choose a career in law.”

The ASBA extends its sincere thanks to the judges for giving their time and expertise, and to the volunteer attorneys, coaches, teachers, court staff and families who made the competition possible. The ASBA also thanks the Department of Education’s Secondary Division, School Lunch Program, Educational Technical Division for their partnership and support.

Building on this first competition, the ASBA is working toward entering a team to represent American Samoa at the 2028 National High School Mock Trial Championship.

The American Samoa Bar Association is the official bar association and licensing body for attorneys practicing law in American Samoa. The ASBA works to promote justice, the rule of law and a strong legal system through public education, legislative review, support for the judiciary and advocacy for the rule of law.

Through programs like the High School Mock Trial Competition, the ASBA works to build understanding of the justice system and encourage the next generation of leaders in the territory.
